lesson.title: Third-party conformity assessment
lesson.summary: Distinguish a legally required third-party route from voluntary testing and the non-safety-risk limit.

prerequisites.reason: The term is introduced as the second condition of the product classification route.
The required assessment route must be traced to the correct sector instrument.

blocks: **Conformity assessment** demonstrates whether specified requirements are met. A third-party assessment involves an external assessment body. The product route asks whether the relevant product is legally required to undergo that route under listed product law.
A voluntary laboratory test or consultant review is not automatically the required statutory third-party assessment. Identify the instrument, product category and mandated route.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 3(20)–(22); Article 6(1)(a), 6(1)(b), 6(1c)

blocks: Article 6(1) joins two conditions: covered AI product or safety component, and the relevant product's required third-party conformity assessment. The AI may be marketed independently of the product; separate supply does not remove the test.

If a fictional case explicitly establishes both conditions, the product-route conclusion follows subject to the statutory qualifications. If the assessment route is missing, the conclusion is conditional.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 3(20)–(22); Article 6(1)(a), 6(1)(b), 6(1c)

blocks: Paragraph 1c says the assessment condition is not met when third-party assessment is required solely for risks other than health and safety, including specified spectrum/interference risks that do not affect health and safety.
The word **solely** again matters. Do not exclude a route involving both safety and non-safety risks merely because spectrum is one reason for assessment.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 3(20)–(22); Article 6(1)(a), 6(1)(b), 6(1c)

blocks: Northbridge asks for the product classification and exact assessment obligation rather than inferring them from 'medical AI' or 'certified'. A real medical-device example requires the medical-device scope and classification rules; a protective-device example requires the protective-equipment rules.

Our course cases stipulate those sector facts when they test Article 6 logic. They do not assign an actual device class from a short description. This keeps a useful legal reasoning exercise separate from an unsupported sector determination.

sources.title: AI Act, 27 July 2026 baseline: Article 3(20)–(22); Article 6(1)(a), 6(1)(b), 6(1c)
